h1: The 7 Best Power Banks of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 power banks scored on capacity, output wattage, ports and carry size, from pocket 10,000mAh packs to laptop-ready Anker units.
summary: The Anker 20,000mAh with 87W output is the best all-rounder, because it can charge a laptop and a phone from one brick. Step up to the Anker Laptop Power Bank for 25,000mAh and triple 100W ports. The INIU 10,000mAh is the pocket pick for phones. Avoid giant capacity numbers unless you truly need a multi-day buffer.
intro: Capacity is the number everyone shops by and the one that misleads most. A 20,000mAh bank is not twice as useful as a 10,000mAh one if its output is too weak to run your laptop or too slow to top up a phone before your train arrives. What decides whether a power bank helps you is the wattage it can deliver and the number of ports it can serve at once.

So we ranked output and ports first, capacity second. Our editors reviewed seven power banks from compact 10,000mAh phone packs to a laptop-capable 25,000mAh unit and a 60,000mAh brick, scoring each on the Primea framework with price kept inside the bucket each one really sells in.

products.name: Anker Power Bank
products.verdict: 87W output and 20,000mAh in one brick, enough for a phone, a tablet and most laptops.
products.description:
This Anker puts 87W of power to share behind a 20,000mAh cell, plus speedy cable charging. Wattage is the real story: 87W is the level where a small laptop can charge from a bank rather than just crawl along.

It beats the Laptop model below on price, since it lands in the $50 to $100 bucket while the other sits at $100 to $200. You give up the third high-wattage port and the built-in cables, but most travellers will not miss either.

Buy it if you carry a laptop and a phone and want a single brick that handles both. The caveat is weight: 20,000mAh is a noticeable chunk in a jacket pocket, so keep it in a bag. If you only ever charge a phone, you are paying for headroom you will not use.
products.idealFor: Commuters carrying a laptop and phone who want one brick.
products.skipIf: You only charge a phone and want pocket size.

products.name: Anker Laptop Power Bank
products.verdict: Triple 100W USB-C ports, 25,000mAh and dual built-in cables for a full workday away from a wall.
products.description:
The Laptop Power Bank has three USB-C ports rated 100W each and 25,000mAh of capacity, along with dual built-in cables. That cable pair matters on a plane or a train, where a snapped or forgotten cable ends the session.

It ranks second because it costs the most here, in the $100 to $200 bucket, and weighs more than the Anker Power Bank. In return you get more capacity and the ability to feed several devices fast, which makes it the better tool for someone who works away from a desk.

Buy it if you regularly work from cafes, planes or job sites. The caveat is that 100W per port does not mean 300W across three, because the bank shares its total output, so check the combined limit before you plug in two laptops at once.
products.idealFor: Remote workers who charge a laptop plus phone on the move.
products.skipIf: You carry only a phone and care about weight.

products.name: INIU 10000mAh 45W Fast Charging Portable Charger
products.verdict: A 45W, 10,000mAh brick that is 40% smaller than rivals and carries a detachable cable.
products.description:
INIU's 10,000mAh bank delivers 45W, which is enough to charge a phone quickly and give a tablet a real top-up. It is described as 40% smaller and lighter, with a detachable cable so one lead serves more than one device.

It ranks third because 45W will not keep a full-size laptop alive the way the Anker pair will, but it costs under $25 and fits in a pocket. For a phone-only owner it is the better buy: you get fast charging without the weight or cost of a big brick.

Buy it for daily carry and the occasional weekend away. The caveat is capacity, since 10,000mAh gives roughly two phone charges at best. Keep the detachable cable with the bank so you do not end up with a bank and no way to use it.
products.idealFor: Daily phone carry where size and price matter most.
products.skipIf: You need to run a full-size laptop.

products.name: INIU Power Bank, Compact 10000mAh 45W PD Fast Charging Portable Charger
products.verdict: A second compact INIU with 45W PD and a lanyard that doubles as the cable.
products.description:
This compact INIU also offers 10,000mAh at 45W with PD fast charging, but its twist is a lanyard that serves as the cable. The pitch is that a power bank only helps if you actually have the cable with you, and a cable looped around your neck or bag solves that.

It ranks below the other INIU because the main model is the proven shape, and a lanyard-cable design adds a weak point where it can fray with daily wear. It still earns a spot because forgetting the cable is the number one reason a bank fails in practice.

Buy it if you are the person who always leaves the cable at home. The caveat is that the lanyard cable is shorter and less flexible than a normal lead, and its life depends on how roughly you treat it.
products.idealFor: Forgetful commuters who keep losing their charging cable.
products.skipIf: You prefer a standard cable you can replace.

products.name: Anker MagGo Power Bank
products.verdict: A slim, matte-finish Anker with versatile charging options for phones.
products.description:
The MagGo is described as slim and portable with versatile charging options and a sleek matte finish. The MagGo name signals magnetic attachment to compatible phones, which turns the bank into a snap-on battery rather than a loose brick with a cable.

It sits fifth because the listing gives no capacity or wattage figure, which makes it hard to rank on raw performance. It beats the Evopow pack on build and brand, but it asks for the same $50 to $100 bucket as the 87W Anker that can charge a laptop.

Buy it if you want a clean, cable-free phone top-up at a desk or on the sofa. The caveat is that magnetic charging is slower than wired charging, so it suits topping up rather than recovering a dead phone.
cons: Costs as much as the 87W model
products.idealFor: Phone owners who prefer snap-on charging to cables.
products.skipIf: You want maximum output per dollar.

products.name: ZZI Portable Charger Power Bank 60000mAh
products.verdict: A huge 60,000mAh store that charges five devices at once, at a slow 22.5W.
products.description:
ZZI offers 60,000mAh, five simultaneous outputs, 22.5W super fast charging and battery protection. That is a lot of energy for the $25 to $50 bucket, enough to keep a family of phones running through a long camping weekend.

It ranks sixth because 22.5W is slow next to the 45W and 87W banks above, and a brick this large is heavy and awkward to carry. Capacity is its only argument, but for off-grid use that argument is strong.

Buy it for camping, power cuts or a shared family charging hub. The caveat is airline rules: very large banks can exceed carry-on limits, so check capacity limits before you fly. It also takes a long time to recharge itself from empty.
products.idealFor: Camping, power cuts and family charging hubs.
products.skipIf: You fly often or carry it daily.

products.name: Evopow 2 Pack Portable Charger
products.verdict: Two slim chargers for the price of one, with three outputs and two inputs.
products.description:
Evopow sells a two-pack of slim chargers with three outputs and two inputs and high-speed charging. A pair means one lives in your bag and one stays at home or in the car, which is a smarter way to avoid being caught short.

It finishes seventh since neither capacity nor wattage is published, so a speed comparison with the INIU is impossible. It wins on sheer count and price, since it is in the under $25 bucket for two units.

Buy it if you want spare banks for kids, a desk drawer or a car. The caveat is the lack of specifics: with no capacity stated, assume modest output and use it for phones rather than tablets or laptops.
products.idealFor: Households wanting spare banks for bags, cars and kids.
products.skipIf: You need a proven fast-charging spec.

methodology.title: Output wattage
methodology.description: Wattage decides what a bank can charge, so units that publish 45W, 87W or 100W figures outranked those that only say fast.

methodology.title: Capacity honesty
methodology.description: We favored capacities that match the device class, since 10,000mAh suits phones while laptops need more power behind more wattage.

methodology.title: Port count and cables
methodology.description: Multiple ports, built-in cables and lanyard leads earned credit because a bank without a cable is not useful.

methodology.title: Carry size
methodology.description: Slim and 40% smaller designs scored higher for daily carry, with heavier units judged by whether the capacity justified the bulk.

methodology.title: Price bucket value
methodology.description: Each bank was weighed inside its stated price range, and listings with few concrete numbers lost points.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage is how fast the bank can push energy out. A phone happily charges at 20W to 45W, a tablet wants 30W or more, and a laptop usually needs 60W or higher. Look for a stated output figure, and check that the number applies to a single port rather than being split across all of them.

Capacity is the size of the tank, measured in milliamp hours at the cell's voltage. A 10,000mAh bank gives roughly two phone charges after conversion losses, while 20,000mAh doubles that. Real delivered capacity is lower than the label, so buy a size above what you think you need.

A bank with three ports can charge three devices, but the total output is shared. Plug in two devices and each may slow down. Check the listing for a combined output figure, not just the per-port number, and look for USB-C ports since they carry the highest wattage.

Many banks ship with no cable, and a bank without one is a brick. Built-in cables or lanyard leads solve that, though a fixed cable cannot be replaced if it breaks. Check whether a cable is included, which connector type it has, and whether a detachable option is offered.

Heavy banks make daily carry unpleasant, and large ones can run into airline limits. Banks are carried in the cabin, and capacity above a certain level may need approval. Check the weight and the watt-hour rating on the listing before a trip, and keep the bank in carry-on luggage.

howToChoose.intro: Start with the hungriest device you carry.

cards.label: Built-in or lanyard cable
cards.text: You always have a lead with you, but a damaged cable cannot be swapped. Picks: Anker Laptop Power Bank and the compact INIU with lanyard.

cards.label: Standard cable
cards.text: Replaceable and flexible, but easy to leave at home. Picks: INIU 10000mAh, Anker Power Bank and ZZI.

howToChoose.note: Default to a standard cable unless you often forget one.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Output of 60W or more per port, USB-C PD support and enough capacity to deliver at least one full charge.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Anker Power Bank at 87W for most laptops, or the Anker Laptop Power Bank with triple 100W ports for heavier use.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You carry a laptop. The Anker Power Bank or the Laptop model delivers wattage that cheaper banks cannot.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only charge a phone. The INIU 10000mAh costs under $25 and gives 45W of fast charging.

faq.q: Can these power banks charge a laptop?
faq.a: The Anker Power Bank at 87W and the Anker Laptop Power Bank with triple 100W ports are the two that can. The INIU at 45W will slowly charge a lightweight laptop, but anything larger will drain faster than the bank supplies.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying a power bank?
faq.a: Buying by capacity alone. The ZZI has 60,000mAh but charges at 22.5W, so it is slower than the 45W INIU for a phone. Match wattage to the device first, then pick a capacity size that fits your day.

faq.q: Is a 60,000mAh bank worth it over a 20,000mAh one?
faq.a: Only for camping, outages or sharing. The ZZI stores three times the energy of the 20,000mAh Anker but is far heavier and slower. For ordinary travel, the Anker Power Bank at 87W is the more useful tool.

faq.q: How do I use a power bank with a magnetic phone?
faq.a: The Anker MagGo is built for magnetic phones, so you snap it on and charging starts. It is slower than a wired connection. For a fast top-up when you are in a hurry, use the cable on a bank like the INIU instead.

faq.q: How should I look after a power bank?
faq.a: Keep it away from heat and recharge it every few months even if unused, because lithium cells lose charge slowly. Avoid leaving the INIU or Anker in a hot car, and stop using any bank that swells or smells.

faq.q: Can I take these on a plane?
faq.a: Power banks go in carry-on, never in checked bags. Most 10,000mAh and 20,000mAh banks like the INIU or Anker are accepted, but a 60,000mAh unit like the ZZI may exceed airline watt-hour limits, so check your airline's rules before you fly.

finalTake: For most people the Anker Power Bank is the right buy, with 87W output and 20,000mAh in the $50 to $100 bucket. Choose the Anker Laptop Power Bank if you work from planes and cafes, and the INIU 10000mAh if you only ever charge a phone. Treat the ZZI as an off-grid tool, not a daily carry, and avoid any bank that cannot tell you its wattage.
